paper_title: Less from More: Reinforcing Sparse Video Reasoning from Dense References

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video-language models commonly assume that more temporal observations lead to more reliable reasoning. We question this assumption and argue that the key challenge is not merely processing more video frames efficiently, but learning to reason reliably under limited temporal evidence. We propose SAVER, a dense-to-sparse post-training framework that uses dense video views as training-time references for sparse-frame inference. During reinforcement post-training, paired dense and sparse views are optimized with grounding rewards and a reliability-gated reference reward, encouraging sparse view predictions to preserve task-relevant temporal evidence. Notably, SAVER is trained only on 1,250 randomly sampled temporal grounding examples, without using any video question answering annotations. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks and six video question-answering benchmarks, SAVER consistently improves performance across frame budgets. In particular, SAVER can match or surpass dense-frame Qwen3.5 baselines while using substantially fewer frames. These results show that temporal grounding can serve as an effective evidence-localization proxy for learning sparse video reasoning that transfers to broader video understanding tasks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A common recipe for improving video reasoning is to show multimodal large language models (MLLMs) more frames. Recent MLLM families, including Qwen-VL (Bai et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025b,a; Team, 2026), InternVL (Chen et al., 2024b,a), and LLaVA-style models (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024a; Lin et al., 2024), have substantially strengthened visual understanding, while video post-training further enhances reasoning on question answering, perception, and temporal tasks (Feng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Feng et al., 2026). Yet most video reasoning pipelines still rely on dense-input assumption: reliable predictions require observing many frames. This assumption is costly, as dense temporal inputs can involve tens or hundreds of frames, leading to large visual-token budgets, high memory usage, and increased latency. Such costs are especially problematic for streaming video, mobile assistants, robotics, surveillance, and long-form video search, where models must operate under limited compute or latency budgets. Efficient video reasoning therefore requires reducing the visual evidence processed in the first place, not merely decoding responses faster. This raises simple but underexplored question: do video-language models truly need dense frame sampling at inference time, or can they be post-trained to reason reliably from sparse temporal observations? The answer is non-trivial. Simply reducing the frame rate lowers visual cost, but it also removes temporal evidence that may be necessary for answering questions or localizing events (Li et al., 2025d). At the same time, dense sampling often introduces substantial redundancy, and its computational cost grows quickly with the number of observed frames. The central challenge we address in this paper is therefore not merely to process dense videos more efficiently, but to make sparse-frame inference itself reliable. Figure 2 Performanceefficiency trade-off across frame rates. Lower frame rates reduce the number of sampled frames but enlarge the sparsedense performance gap for Qwen3.5. SAVER mitigates this degradation; for example, for video-QA, SAVER-2B at 0.1 fps nearly matches dense Qwen3.5-2B at 2.0 fps. Figure 2 illustrates the accuracyframe-budget trade-off. Lowering the frame rate reduces the number of sampled frames substantially, but it also degrades standard Qwen3.5 models, especially on temporal grounding where accurate localization depends on sufficient temporal evidence. SAVER changes this trade-off: at the same frame rate, it consistently improves over Qwen3.5, and at lower frame rates it can approach the accuracy of denser Qwen3.5 inference while using far fewer frames. For example, on video-QA benchmarks, SAVER-2B at 0.1 fps nearly matches Qwen3.5-2B at 2.0 fps. Importantly, this improvement transfers from temporal grounding, the task used for post-training, to six video-QA benchmarks, suggesting that learning to preserve temporal evidence under sparse observations benefits broader video reasoning. Existing efficiency approaches only partially address this problem. Some methods accelerate reasoning on the language side, for example by reducing redundant decoding or reasoning steps (Liu et al., 2026a), but they do not directly reduce the cost of visual input processing. Other methods reduce visual computation through token compression (Wu et al., 2025), adaptive keyframe sampling (Tang et al., 2025), or retrieval-based frame selection (Zou et al., 2026). These approaches are effective, but they typically assume richer visual input and then reduce its cost by compressing, selecting, or retrieving visual evidence. Our work addresses different part of the efficiency problem: given prescribed low-frame-rate visual budget, can the video-language model itself be made reliable under sparse temporal evidence? In this work, we study sparse video reasoning: the model receives only sparsely sampled frames at inference time and must reason reliably under limited temporal evidence. Sparse observations may miss key events, provide coarse temporal boundaries, or emphasize misleading static cues, making models trained mainly under dense observations fragile when the frame budget is reduced. Rather than designing another frame selector or token compressor, we take training-centric view: dense frames should serve as training-time references for learning sparse-frame reasoning, but should not be required at inference time. Motivated by this view, we propose SAVER, dense-guided sparse post-training framework for efficient video understanding. SAVER constructs paired dense and sparse views from the same video and uses temporal grounding as an evidence-localization proxy task. Dense views provide richer temporal reference signals, while sparse view predictions are optimized with grounding rewards and reference reward that aligns them with reliable dense view predictions. Notably, SAVER is trained only on 1,250 randomly sampled temporal grounding examples from Time-R1 (Wang et al., 2025), without using any video-QA annotations. Despite this small grounding-only training set, SAVER consistently improves across three temporal grounding benchmarks and six video question-answering benchmarks under different frame budgets, with particularly strong gains in the sparse regime. These results suggest that efficient video reasoning should not only focus on compressing dense-frame inference, but also on training models to remain reliable when dense temporal evidence is unavailable.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Visual reasoning models. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced image and video understanding. Representative model families include Qwen-VL (Bai et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025b,a; Team, 2026), InternVL (Chen et al., 2024b,a), LLaVA-style models (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024a), and video-oriented MLLMs such as Video-LLaVA (Lin et al., 2024), VideoChat (Li et al., 2025b), and TimeChat (Ren et al., 2024). Building on these models, reinforcement post-training has become popular strategy for improving visual reasoning. VisionReasoner (Liu et al., 2026b) and RegionReasoner (Sun et al., 2026) focus on image-level and region-grounded reasoning, while Video-R1 (Feng et al., 2025), VideoChat-R1 (Li et al., 2025c), VideoAuto-R1 (Liu et al., 2026a), and OneThinker (Feng et al., 2026) extend reasoning-oriented post-training to video. Other works further investigate temporal grounding (Wang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a), video reasoning segmentation (Gong et al., 2025), frame-referenced reasoning traces (Ghazanfari et al., 2025), and scalable video reasoning training (Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025e; Fu et al., 2025b). These methods improve the models reasoning behavior or supervision signal, but generally assume that sufficient visual evidence is available at inference time. In contrast, our work studies whether video reasoning can remain reliable when only sparse temporal observations are provided at test time. Efficient video understanding. The high computational cost of video understanding has motivated methods that reduce either language-side or visual-side computation. Language-side methods reduce redundant reasoning or decoding steps; for example, VideoAuto-R1 (Liu et al., 2026a) avoids unnecessary repeated reasoning, while Sparse-to-Dense (Zhang et al., 2025b) accelerates decoding through sparse-attention speculation and denseattention verification. Visual-side methods reduce the cost of processing long or dense videos by compressing visual tokens or selecting informative frames. MARC (Wu et al., 2025) studies memory-augmented token compression for efficient video understanding, STORM (Jiang et al., 2025) reduces visual tokens for long-video MLLMs, and frame selection or retrieval methods such as M-LLM-based frame selection (Hu et al., 2025a), Adaptive Keyframe Sampling (Tang et al., 2025), Generative Frame Sampler (Yao et al., 2025), VideoBrain (Zou et al., 2026), and ReViSe (Xu et al., 2026) select or retrieve useful frames from richer video contexts. QFrame (Zhang et al., 2025a) further combines query-aware frame selection with multi-resolution adaptation. FastVID (Shen et al., 2025) dynamically prunes redundant visual information, while WFS-SB (Chen et al., 2026) selects informative frames by detecting semantic boundaries. These works show that not all frames or visual tokens contribute equally to video understanding. Our setting differs in that we evaluate the model under fixed low-frame-rate input budget: the model receives only uniformly sampled sparse frames at inference time, rather than first accessing richer video representation and then selecting or compressing it. Accordingly, SAVER does not propose new frame selector or token compressor; instead, it uses dense views only during training as scaffolds and aligns sparse view predictions with dense view signals through reinforcement post-training. This targets different question: how can video model remain reliable when dense temporal evidence is unavailable or too costly to process at inference time?

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: SAVER targets efficient video inference under low-frame-rate protocol. At test time, the model receives frames at prescribed fps and predicts from this sparse input. It does not perform dense video pre-scanning, adaptive frame selection, or test-time optimization. Thus, the goal is not to introduce sampling strategy, but to make the model reliable when only sparse frames are processed.

sections.title: 3.1 Overview
sections.content: For each training example, SAVER follows three simple steps. First, we sample two views from the same video: dense view with more frames and sparse view with fewer frames. Second, both views are fed into the same MLLM policy πθ, producing dense view response yd and sparse view response ys. Third, we optimize both responses with temporal grounding rewards and add dense-to-sparse reference reward, so that the sparse prediction learns from the dense prediction only when the dense prediction is more reliable. After training, only the sparse view is used for inference. sections.title: 3.2 Dense-to-Sparse Post-Training
sections.content: SAVER performs reinforcement post-training with paired dense and sparse video views, where dense views provide training-time guidance for improving sparse-frame inference. We use temporal grounding as the training task because it provides explicit supervision over when an event occurs, making it natural signal for learning task-relevant temporal evidence. In our implementation, we randomly sample 1,250 training examples from Time-R1 (Wang et al., 2025). No video-QA annotations are used during post-training. Therefore, improvements on video-QA benchmarks come from cross-task transfer rather than task-specific QA post-training. We then use the dense prediction as training-time reference for the sparse prediction only when the dense view is more reliable. This dense-to-sparse alignment encourages the sparse view to preserve temporal evidence that is available in the dense view, while avoiding imitation of unreliable dense predictions.

This makes the inference protocol compatible with low-fps streaming or resource-constrained settings, where only sparse frame stream is decoded or processed. Relation to distillation and risk intuition. SAVER is related to self-distillation, but differs in both the input views and the use of the teacher signal. Conventional self-distillation usually transfers predictions under the same input distribution, whereas SAVER performs reward-guided cross-view distillation from dense temporal views to sparse temporal views. The dense view provides privileged training-time information, while the sparse view matches the inference-time condition. Importantly, dense predictions are not treated as unconditional pseudo-labels: the alignment reward is activated only when the dense view grounding reward is higher than the sparse view grounding reward. This prevents sparse predictions from imitating inferior dense view outputs. This view also gives simple risk-decomposition intuition for dense-to-sparse alignment. This inequality suggests that sparse view performance depends on two factors: the reliability of dense view predictions and the discrepancy between sparse view and dense view predictions. SAVER directly targets both factors. The grounding rewards improve the quality of predictions under each view, while the relative reliability-gated reference reward reduces the sparsedense discrepancy only when the dense view provides better temporal reference. Thus, dense frames are used not to increase test-time computation, but to provide reliable training-time guidance for sparse-frame inference.

sections.title: 4.1 Experiment Details
sections.content: Implementation details. We instantiate SAVER on Qwen3.5 (Team, 2026) models with three different scales: 0.8B, 2B, and 4B. All models are trained with the same densesparse reinforcement post-training framework described in Sec. 3. Unlike large-scale video reasoning post-training methods, SAVER uses only small temporal grounding training set. Specifically, we randomly sample 1,250 examples from Time-R1 (Wang et al., 2025) and use them as the only post-training data. No video-QA annotations are used during post-training, allowing us to evaluate whether sparse temporal alignment learned from grounding supervision transfers to broader video understanding tasks. For each training example, we construct dense view and sparse view from the same video. Both views are fed into the same policy model, and the model is optimized with grounding rewards and dense-to-sparse reference rewards. We set the coefficient of the sparse view reward to 2.0 to emphasize sparse-frame robustness, and set all other reward coefficients to 1.0. For reinforcement learning, the rollout size is set to = 4. The global batch sizes are set to 64, 64, and 128 for the 0.8B, 2B, and 4B models. We train the 0.8B, 2B, and 4B models using 16, 16, and 32 A100 GPUs, with training times of approximately 4, 7, and 13 hours, respectively. We will release the code, model checkpoints, and sampled training subset to facilitate reproducibility. Evaluation protocol. At test time, SAVER directly operates on sparsely sampled frames without using dense video inputs. We control the visual budget by varying the sampling frame rate over {0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2} fps. This protocol allows us to evaluate the performanceefficiency trade-off from extremely sparse observations to denser temporal inputs. We cap the number of sampled frames to [4, 256] per video for fair comparison. For each fps setting, we report both task performance and the corresponding average number of sampled frames. We evaluate with lmms-eval (Zhang et al., 2024) using greedy decoding unless noted. Evaluation benchmarks. Following prior video reasoning evaluation protocols (Liu et al., 2026a), we evaluate SAVER on temporal grounding and video question answering benchmarks. For temporal grounding, we evaluate on Charades-STA (Gao et al., 2017) and ActivityNet (Caba Heilbron et al., 2015), reporting mean temporal intersection-over-union (mIoU). We further evaluate on NExT-GQA (Xiao et al., 2024), which combines question answering with temporal grounding and requires models to identify task-relevant video segments. Beyond the grounding task used for post-training, we evaluate transfer to video-QA benchmarks. For perception-oriented video-QA, we report accuracy on VideoMME without subtitles (Fu et al., 2025a), MVBench (Li et al., 2024b), LongVideoBench (Wu et al., 2024), and MMVU (Zhao et al., 2025). For reasoning-intensive video understanding, we evaluate on VideoMMMU (Hu et al., 2025b) and Minimal Video Pairs (MVP) (Krojer et al., 2025).

We first evaluate temporal grounding because it is the task used for post-training and directly measures whether the model can localize task-relevant temporal evidence. This is reflected in the original Qwen3.5 baselines. sections.title: 4.3 Analysis
sections.content: Reward ablation. Table 3 reports reward ablations using Qwen3.5-2B evaluated at 0.1 fps. Joint dense-andsparse training obtains 27.4 mIoU and 48.7% average video-QA accuracy, exceeding either single-view variant. Adding the reference reward increases these scores to 29.1 and 49.3%, respectively. The gated variant obtains the highest scores in this comparison, reaching 30.0 mIoU and 50.8% average video-QA accuracy. These ablations show incremental gains from the reference reward and its relative-quality gate under the evaluated configuration. Comparison with alternative training strategies. We compare alternative post-training strategies in Table 4. All variants use the same Qwen3.5-2B initialization and 1,250 grounding examples and are evaluated at 0.1 fps. Time-R1 RL uses 2.0-fps training inputs and obtains 21.0 mIoU and 49.1% average video-QA accuracy. Sparse SFT uses 0.5-fps inputs with either ground-truth segments or fixed pseudo-labels generated by the original model at 2.0 fps, obtaining 20.3 and 19.6 mIoU, respectively. SAVER achieves the highest scores among these evaluated configurations, with 30.0 mIoU and 50.8% average video-QA accuracy. Replacing the dense reference with the ground-truth segment gives 29.5 mIoU and 50.1% average video-QA accuracy. The two reference variants perform similarly on grounding, while the dense-reference variant obtains modestly higher QA score in this comparison. These results support the effectiveness of the proposed training configuration; the mechanism underlying its cross-task transfer remains an open question. 8 Figure 3 Qualitative comparison under sparse observations. Figure 4 shows the effect of the sparse view reward weight λs at 0.1 fps, where sparse-frame inference is most challenging. small value of λs provides insufficient pressure for the model to improve sparse-frame robustness, leading to weaker performance under limited frame budgets. Increasing λs improves both sparse view temporal grounding mIoU and video-QA accuracy, showing that explicitly emphasizing the sparse view is important for sparse video reasoning. However, an overly large weight can overemphasize sparse view rewards and weaken the balance between dense view scaffolding and sparse view optimization. We therefore set λs = 2 as the default, which achieves the best overall trade-off across temporal grounding and video-QA. We further analyze the sensitivity to the reference reward weight λref in Appendix E, where the results show an optimal intermediate weighting rather than monotonic gains from increasing the reward magnitude. While SAVER improves sparse-frame inference across benchmarks, it does not eliminate all failures under limited temporal evidence. We observe two common failure modes. First, when the sparse frames completely miss the key event, the model may still predict an overly broad or shifted temporal interval. Second, when visually similar actions occur multiple times in video, the model may align to the 9 wrong occurrence, especially under very low frame rates. We provide additional success and failure cases in the Appendix H. promising future direction is adaptive online sampling, where the model can request additional frames when sparse observations are insufficient.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented SAVER, dense-to-sparse reinforcement post-training framework for sparse-input video understanding. The framework jointly trains dense and sparse views with grounding supervision and uses relative-quality gate to control an interval-level reference reward. Using 1,250 grounding examples and no videoQA annotations during post-training, SAVER improves macro-averaged performance across the evaluated model scales and frame budgets. Its video-QA results demonstrate cross-task transfer, although the magnitude and direction of the gains vary across benchmarks. Importantly, inference requires neither dense video pre-scanning nor adaptive frame selection or test-time optimization, preserving fixed sparse-input protocol. Rather than selecting more informative frames at inference time, SAVER learns to make better use of limited temporal evidence through post-training. These findings support training-time dense references as practical approach to improving performance under limited temporal observations.

We further compare the practical inference cost of SAVER, FastVID, and WFS-SB under matched profiling settings, using the Qwen3.5-2B backbone and averaging over the three benchmarks in Table 9. Table 10 reports visual-token count, peak GPU memory, GPU inference latency and end-to-end latency. The practical-cost comparison further highlights the different inference trade-offs. SAVER processes fewer visual tokens and uses less peak GPU memory than the two selection-based methods, while also requiring lower GPU inference latency and end-to-end latency under the matched profiling setting. This advantage follows from the different inference pipeline: SAVER improves sparse-input capability during post-training and therefore does not require dense pre-scanning, intermediate feature extraction, or an additional selection stage at inference time. FastVID and WFS-SB instead spend additional inference-time computation to identify informative visual content from richer candidate representation. Such processing can be worthwhile when richer input pool is available, as demonstrated by the improved performance of SAVER + WFS-SB in Table 9. Taken together, these results suggest that SAVER provides complementary training-time approach to efficient video reasoning: it reduces the models dependence on dense observations, while adaptive selection methods can further improve the sparse input when additional inference-time computation is available.

sections.title: E Effect of Reference Reward Weight
sections.content: We study the sensitivity of SAVER to the reference reward coefficient λref . This analysis examines whether the observed gains can be explained simply by increasing the relative contribution of the reference reward during optimization. All results use Qwen3.5-2B and are evaluated at 0.1 fps. As shown in Table 11, reward weighting affects performance, but the gains are not explained by monotonically increasing the reference reward weight. Starting from λref = 0, introducing the reference objective substantially improves both temporal grounding and video-QA. Performance improves as λref increases to 1.0, whereas further increasing it to 2.0 yields only marginal improvement in temporal grounding (30.0 to 30.1 mIoU) while reducing video-QA accuracy from 50.8 to 50.2. These results indicate that the reference reward contributes distinct cross-view alignment objective, while λref controls the strength of this objective during optimization. Effect of Grounding Post-Training Data Scale We study the effect of the grounding post-training data scale in Table 12. Time-R1 contains approximately 2500 temporal grounding training examples, while our main experiments use only randomly sampled subset of 1250 examples. We observe that increasing the amount of grounding supervision initially improves both temporal grounding and video-QA performance. However, the gains saturate beyond 1250 examples, and using the full 2500-example training set slightly degrades performance under sparse inference. We hypothesize that excessive grounding-focused post-training may over-specialize the model toward narrow localization patterns and reduce the diversity of temporal reasoning behaviors. Overall, these results suggest that effective dense-to-sparse reasoning transfer can emerge from relatively small amount of grounding supervision. Confidence-Based Sparse-to-Dense Fallback SAVER is designed for direct sparse-frame inference and does not require dense video access at test time. Nevertheless, when additional computation is available, the sparse prediction can optionally be used to decide whether denser observation should be requested. We therefore study simple confidence-based sparse-to-dense fallback strategy. We first perform inference using sparse frames sampled at 0.1 fps. If the confidence of the sparse prediction falls below threshold γ, we rerun the same example using frames sampled at 2.0 fps and use the dense-view prediction instead. Table 13 reports the resulting performancecomputation trade-off for temporal grounding and video-QA. As γ increases, more examples are routed to dense inference, increasing the average frame budget and generally moving performance toward the dense-view setting. However, the fallback strategy does not improve performance monotonically. At lower thresholds, the confidence signal is not sufficiently calibrated to identify examples that truly require additional temporal evidence. As result, some correct sparse predictions are replaced by less helpful dense predictions, leading to degraded temporal-grounding performance. At γ = 0.7, the fallback strategy improves temporal grounding from 30.0 to 38.3 average mIoU and video-QA from 50.8 to 52.0 average accuracy, while processing substantially fewer frames than dense-only inference (47 vs. 110 frames for temporal grounding and 54 vs. 139 frames for video-QA). These results indicate that selective access to denser observations can provide additional gains when sparse evidence is insufficient, but its effectiveness depends critically on reliable confidence calibration. We therefore treat confidence-based fallback as an optional extension rather than part of the default SAVER inference protocol.

sections.title: H Additional Qualitative Cases
sections.content: We provide additional qualitative examples for both temporal grounding and video question answering under the extremely sparse inference setting of 0.1 fps. Figures 5 and 6 show Charades-STA grounding cases, where SAVER predicts temporal segments from sparse frames. Figures 7 and 8 show VideoMMMU cases, where SAVER must solve reasoning-intensive video questions from sparse observations. Together, these examples show that SAVER can preserve task-relevant evidence when the sampled frames contain sufficient cues, but may still fail when the sparse observations miss critical information or when the reasoning chain contains an incorrect intermediate assumption. 19 Figure 5 Temporal grounding success case on Charades-STA. Given the query person opens small cabinet door, SAVER correctly identifies that the action starts at the beginning of the clip and ends around 4 seconds. The predicted interval closely matches the ground-truth segment, showing that sparse-frame reasoning can succeed when the sampled frames preserve the key temporal evidence. 20 Figure 6 Temporal grounding failure case on Charades-STA. Given the query person throws their blanket inside, SAVER predicts an earlier interval than the ground truth. Although the reasoning identifies plausible moment when the person moves near the doorway, the sparse observations do not provide enough evidence to precisely distinguish the target throwing action. This example highlights common failure mode: sparse-frame inference can still localize an incorrect segment when the key action is ambiguous or insufficiently captured. Figure 7 Video-QA success case on VideoMMMU. Given mechanics question about how the vertical displacement changes when the length increases from 2 inches to 3 inches, SAVER correctly follows the visual solution and derives the proportional change. The model identifies the relevant formula, applies the new length, and selects the correct answer, showing that sparse video reasoning can succeed when the sampled frames retain the necessary visual and textual evidence. 22 Figure 8 Video-QA failure case on VideoMMMU. Given chemistry question about the mass of oxygen corresponding to 4 kg of hydrogen atoms, SAVER applies the standard hydrogen-to-oxygen mass ratio in water (1:8) and selects (32 kg), whereas the ground-truth answer is (64 kg), which corresponds to 1:16 mass relation. Although the arithmetic is internally consistent, the model relies on default prior assumption instead of the relation presented in the video. This example shows that sparse video reasoning can still fail when the reasoning chain is built on an incorrect premise that is not grounded in the visual evidence.
